subject: Mathematics Foundations to Computer Science - I

questions.topic: Sets, set operations, Venn diagrams and Cartesian products
questions.text: What is the Cartesian product of two sets?
questions.ideal_answer: The Cartesian product of sets A and B, written A cross B, is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) where a belongs to A and b belongs to B. For example, if A = {1, 2} and B = {x, y}, then A cross B = {(1, x), (1, y), (2, x), (2, y)}. If A has m elements and B has n elements, the product has m times n elements. In general A cross B is not equal to B cross A because the pairs are ordered.

questions.topic: Counting, pigeonhole principle, permutations and combinations
questions.ideal_answer: The pigeonhole principle states that if n items are placed into m containers and n is greater than m, then at least one container must hold more than one item. For example, among any 13 people, at least two were born in the same month. The generalised form says that at least one container holds at least the ceiling of n divided by m items. It is used to prove existence results in counting and computer science, such as collisions in hashing.

questions.topic: Counting, pigeonhole principle, permutations and combinations
questions.text: What is the difference between a permutation and a combination? Give an example.
questions.ideal_answer: A permutation is an arrangement of objects where order matters, while a combination is a selection where order does not matter. The number of permutations of r objects from n is nPr = n! / (n - r)!, and the number of combinations is nCr = n! / (r! (n - r)!). For example, choosing a president and secretary from 5 students is a permutation, giving 5P2 = 20 ways. Choosing a 2-member committee from 5 students is a combination, giving 5C2 = 10 ways.

questions.topic: Exponential, logarithmic, ceiling and floor functions
questions.text: What are the floor and ceiling functions? Give values for 3.7 and -3.7.
questions.ideal_answer: The floor function gives the greatest integer less than or equal to x, and the ceiling function gives the smallest integer greater than or equal to x. For 3.7, floor is 3 and ceiling is 4. For -3.7, floor is -4 and ceiling is -3. For an integer, floor and ceiling are both equal to the number itself.

questions.topic: Functions: injective, surjective, bijective, inverse and composition
questions.text: Is the function f(x) = 2x + 3 from real numbers to real numbers a bijection? Find its inverse.
questions.ideal_answer: A function is a bijection if it is both injective (one-to-one) and surjective (onto). f(x) = 2x + 3 is injective because if 2a + 3 = 2b + 3 then a = b. It is surjective because for any real y, x = (y - 3)/2 is a real number with f(x) = y. Since it is a bijection, its inverse exists and is f inverse of y = (y - 3)/2.

questions.text: Using the binomial theorem, expand (x + y) to the power 3 and explain where the coefficients come from.
questions.ideal_answer: The binomial theorem says (x + y) to the power n equals the sum of nCk times x to the power (n - k) times y to the power k, for k from 0 to n. For n = 3 the expansion is x cubed + 3 x squared y + 3 x y squared + y cubed. The coefficients 1, 3, 3, 1 are the binomial coefficients 3C0, 3C1, 3C2 and 3C3. They can also be read from the fourth row of Pascal's triangle.

questions.topic: Relations, equivalence relations, closures and Warshall's algorithm
questions.text: Is the relation 'a is congruent to b modulo 3' on integers an equivalence relation? Explain why.
questions.ideal_answer: Yes, it is an equivalence relation because it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. It is reflexive since a minus a = 0 is divisible by 3. It is symmetric because if 3 divides a minus b, then 3 also divides b minus a. It is transitive because if 3 divides a minus b and b minus c, it divides their sum a minus c, and the relation splits the integers into three equivalence classes with remainders 0, 1 and 2.

questions.topic: Recurrence relations: Fibonacci, Tower of Hanoi, characteristic roots
questions.text: Write the recurrence for the Tower of Hanoi and explain why it needs 2 to the power n minus 1 moves.
questions.ideal_answer: To move n discs, we move the top n - 1 discs to the auxiliary peg, move the largest disc to the target peg, then move the n - 1 discs onto it. This gives the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n - 1) + 1 with T(1) = 1. Unrolling gives T(n) = 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2 to the power (n - 1), which is a geometric series summing to 2 to the power n minus 1. For example, 3 discs need 7 moves.

questions.topic: Graph theory basics: paths, cycles, Euler and Hamiltonian graphs
questions.text: How can you decide whether a connected graph has an Euler circuit or an Euler path, and why is the Hamiltonian problem harder?
questions.ideal_answer: A connected graph has an Euler circuit if and only if every vertex has even degree. It has an Euler path but not a circuit if exactly two vertices have odd degree, and the path must start and end at those two vertices. This test is easy and runs in polynomial time. In contrast, there is no simple necessary and sufficient condition for a Hamiltonian cycle, which visits every vertex exactly once, and deciding it is NP-complete, though sufficient conditions like Dirac's theorem exist.

questions.topic: Matrix algebra: determinant, rank and inverse
questions.text: When does a square matrix not have an inverse, and how does this relate to its rank and determinant?
questions.ideal_answer: A square matrix has an inverse only if its determinant is non-zero; such a matrix is called non-singular. If the determinant is zero, the matrix is singular and has no inverse. For an n by n matrix, a zero determinant means its rank is less than n, so its rows or columns are linearly dependent. Then a system Ax = b has either no solution or infinitely many solutions, never a unique one.

questions.topic: Trees, spanning trees and planar graphs
questions.text: A company wants to connect 6 office buildings with network cable at minimum total cost. How would you model and solve this problem?
questions.ideal_answer: Model the buildings as vertices of a weighted graph and possible cable routes as edges with the cable cost as weight. The required network is a minimum spanning tree, which connects all vertices with no cycles and minimum total weight, using exactly n - 1 = 5 edges. It can be found using Kruskal's algorithm, which adds the cheapest edges that do not form a cycle, or Prim's algorithm, which grows the tree from one vertex. In practice one may add a few redundant links for fault tolerance, trading extra cost for reliability.

questions.text: A program needs to solve a system of three linear equations in three unknowns. Compare solving it using the inverse matrix method versus Gaussian elimination.
questions.ideal_answer: The system can be written as AX = B. In the inverse method we compute A inverse and get X = A inverse times B, which needs the determinant to be non-zero. Gaussian elimination reduces the augmented matrix to row echelon form and then uses back substitution. In practice Gaussian elimination is preferred because it needs fewer operations, is more numerically stable, and can also detect when there is no solution or infinitely many solutions by comparing the ranks of A and the augmented matrix.
